title: Build the square
shortDesc: Ordinal square, swap corners, then fold
longDesc: Write 1 through 9 in reading order. Swap each corner with its opposite, 1↔9 and 3↔7, and the cross stays put. Fold that diamond into the square and the Lo Shu appears. Then each property overlays a different arithmetic truth on the same 3×3.

title: Opposites balance
longDesc: Every number has an antipode through the center cell 5. The four pairs are 1+9, 2+8, 3+7, 4+6. Each sums to 10, exactly twice the center. In Chinese cosmology this is yin-yang mirrored: the center holds, the periphery balances.

title: Five rules everything
longDesc: The Lo Shu is governed by 5. All nine numbers sum to 45 = 9×5. Any opposite pair sums to 10 = 2×5. Any row, column or diagonal sums to 15 = 3×5. 5 is not just center — it is the arithmetic mean, median, and divisor of every symmetry.

title: Corners = Edges
longDesc: Add the four corners (all even) you get 20. Add the four edge-centers (all odd except center) you get 20. Parity balances perfectly around 5. It is why the Lo Shu was seen as a model of agricultural equity: corners (fields) equal edges (boundaries).

title: Mirrored distance
longDesc: Subtract 5 from each cell. You get +4,+3,+2,+1 on one side and -1,-2,-3,-4 on the other, mirrored through center. The distance from 5 is preserved but sign flips. This is the zero-balance in disguise.

title: Zero-balanced form
formula: M₀ = M - 5  →  all lines sum to 0
longDesc: If you center the square at zero by subtracting 5 everywhere, the Lo Shu becomes [-1,4,-3; -2,0,2; 3,-4,1]. Every row, column and diagonal now sums to 0. The magic becomes equilibrium: positive and negative cancel around void.

title: Middle is mean
formula: (a + a')/2 = 5 for any line through center
longDesc: Take any line that passes through the center — two diagonals, middle row, middle column. The average of its two ends is exactly the center 5. The center is not inserted; it emerges as the arithmetic mean of its opposites.

title: Lines sum to 15
longDesc: The classic definition: all three rows, three columns and two diagonals sum to 15. Eight lines, one constant. 15 is the smallest possible magic constant for numbers 1-9 using each once.

title: 111 property
longDesc: Read each row as a three-digit number: 492, 357, 816. Sum = 1665. Read each column as 438, 951, 276. Sum = 1665 too. And 1665 = 15 × 111. The magic constant multiplied by the repdigit reveals hidden decimal symmetry.

title: Determinant 360
longDesc: The determinant of the Lo Shu matrix is 360. That's 3×4×5×6, or 9×40, a highly composite number. Meanwhile 9! = 362880 contains 360. The Lo Shu sits at the edge of factorial growth — order emerging from permutation space. Reflections flip the sign to −360.

title: Clockwise addition mod10
longDesc: Travel clockwise around the border starting at 1 (bottom middle). Add the next corner: 1+6=7 (right middle). 7+2=9 (top middle). 9+4=13→3 (left middle). 3+8=11→1 (back). The tens digit falls away, leaving a mod-10 clock that generates the whole perimeter from just two seeds.

title: Counterclockwise arms
longDesc: Going counterclockwise, center 5 plus an edge gives the next corner modulo 10: 5+7=12→2 (top right), 5+9=14→4 (top left), 5+3=8 (bottom left), 5+1=6 (bottom right). The center reaches out and builds corners from edges.

title: Subtraction =5
longDesc: Reverse C: subtract the corner from the following edge clockwise. 9-4=5, 7-2=5, 3-8=-5→5 mod10, 1-6=-5→5 mod10. The constant difference is exactly the center. Addition creates the border; subtraction reveals the center.

title: Knight's tour (torus)
formula: 1→2→3, 7→8→9 = knight (2+1) steps; middle hops are short
longDesc: On the plain grid, 1→2→3 and 7→8→9 are each a chess knight's move from the next, while 3→4→5→6→7 are short orthogonal or diagonal steps. On a torus (wrap edges) every hop reads as a (1,2) offset, which collapses into diagonals — so the honest claim is the narrowed one. The ends of the square trace a knight; the middle walks.

title: All 3×3 are Lo Shu
longDesc: There is essentially one 3×3 normal magic square. All eight variants are just rotations and reflections of Lo Shu — the dihedral group D₄. What looks like many squares is one square seen from eight directions.

title: Eight triples only
formula: 8 subsets of {1…9} sum to 15, and they are the 8 lines
longDesc: List every three distinct integers from 1 to 9 that add to 15. There are eight: 4+9+2, 3+5+7, 8+1+6, 4+3+8, 9+5+1, 2+7+6, 4+5+6, and 2+5+8. Each one is a row, a column, or a diagonal of the square, and every line of the square is one of them. Count the triples each digit belongs to and the seats fall out: 5 belongs to four, so it is the center; 2, 4, 6, and 8 belong to three, so they are the corners; 1, 3, 7, and 9 belong to two, so they are the edges.

title: Products agree
shortDesc: Row products and column products total 225
formula: Σ row products = Σ column products = 225 = 15²
longDesc: Multiply along each row: 4×9×2 = 72, 3×5×7 = 105, and 8×1×6 = 48. The three products add to 225. The columns give 4×3×8 = 96, 9×5×1 = 45, and 2×7×6 = 84, and those add to 225 as well. 225 is 15². One step down, the pairwise products inside the rows add to 195, and the pairwise products inside the columns add to 195. The two diagonals multiply to 4×5×6 + 2×5×8 = 200.

title: Opposite squares match
shortDesc: Outer rows square to 101, columns to 89
formula: opposite outer line: Σ(10−n)² = Σ n²
longDesc: The bottom row is the top row with each cell sent to its complement 10−n, and the right column is the complement of the left. Squaring keeps the total: 4²+9²+2² = 8²+1²+6² = 101, and 4²+3²+8² = 2²+7²+6² = 89. A line through the center is its own complement. Those four square-sums are 77, 93, 83, and 107.

title: Reversed squares
shortDesc: A line and its digit reversal square to the same total
longDesc: Read each row as a three-digit number, 492, 357, and 816. The sum of their squares equals the sum of the squares of the reversals 294, 753, and 618: both are 1,035,369. The columns 438, 951, and 276 do the same and total 1,172,421. The main-diagonal wraps 456, 978, and 231 total 1,217,781. The anti-diagonal wraps 258, 471, and 936 total 1,164,501; on this orientation the anti-diagonal reads 471. Drop any one digit place — the hundreds, the tens, or the units — and each of the four identities still holds. Dropping those places from the rows leaves 11,969, then 10,529, then 10,187.

title: Squared matrix
shortDesc: M² has a constant diagonal; each row is 15²
formula: M² diagonal is constant; each row sums to 15²
longDesc: Multiply the square by itself. On this orientation the main diagonal of M² is 59 and every other entry is 83, and each row sums to 225, which is 15². All eight rotations and reflections keep a constant main diagonal and one other value. The pair is 59 and 83 when the matrix diagonal is the 4–5–6 line, and 91 and 67 when it is the 2–5–8 line. The row sum stays 225 either way. Property P also ends at 225, by multiplying the entries of each line. Here the matrix is multiplied by itself.

title: Nested palaces
shortDesc: Each cell opens into the same 3×3
longDesc: Replace each cell by the Lo Shu shifted by nine times one less than the cell you opened. On this orientation palace 4 opens to 31 36 29 / 30 32 34 / 35 28 33, and each of its lines is 96. Palace 7 opens to 58 63 56 / 57 59 61 / 62 55 60, and each of its lines is 177. The nine blocks use 1 through 81 once; every row, column, and both diagonals sum to 369. Opposite cells through the center sum to 82. The address 3-7 is 25, and the center of the centers is 41, the mean of 1…81. One more depth has 729 cells and sums to 9855, with center 365. The next has 6,561 cells and sums to 265761, with center 3281. Inside palace P the lines are 27·(P−1)+15 and the opposite cells sum to 18·(P−1)+10. The board can zoom down the center path: palace 5 re-centers on 41 and opens the middle third of the 27×27, whose rows sum to 3285; the center 365 re-centers the board and opens the middle third of the 81×81, whose rows sum to 29529.
